M1: Machine names nest one container level only; a name with more than one container level is refused.
M2: Only the container type `lxd` is supported in 4.1; a designation or constraint naming another type is refused.
M3: Constraints that name a container type or a space that does not exist are refused as invalid machine constraints.
M4: Setting constraints on a machine whose recorded instance has a different architecture is refused; only architecture is compared.
M5: Importing a machine whose name the target model already holds fails with "machine already exists".
M6: A lookup of a machine by UUID or name that matches nothing fails with "machine not found".
M7: Asking the reboot logic about a machine whose parent itself has a parent fails with "grandparent machine are not supported currently".
M8: Reprovisioning a machine is refused while its agent is still present.
M9: A machine has one primary record with an internal id and a name that is unique per model.
M10: A container machine is linked to its host machine by a parent record holding two pointers; other parts of Juju (removal, status, network, recovery) also read this record.
M11: A machine's cloud instance record holds creation state, hardware and zone; many other parts of Juju (removal, status, storage, network, migration, recovery) read it.
M12: The compute provisioner watches unprovisioned machines, requests instances from the cloud and records the instance id.
M13: The host machine's agent provisions its local LXD containers through the LXD broker.
M14: Reprovisioning a machine whose cloud instance was lost keeps the machine identity, gives its units new ordinals and provisions a replacement instance; it runs from the client through the API to the controller.
M15: Removing a machine marks it dying and schedules a removal job; the machine becomes dead only when it hosts no containers, units or storage.
M16: Machine watchers report life changes of a machine and its containers to the workers that need them.
M17: A machine designation such as `0`, `lxd:25` or `0/lxd/4` is parsed by the client and again by the controller.
C1: The controller configuration is stored as records that several parts of Juju read (provisioning, key updating, migration).
C2: Each controller node (one per HA node) has a record that many parts of Juju (agent passwords, upgrades, model agents, the change stream) read.
C3: The API address setter recomputes the controller's API addresses when the network changes.
C4: The certificate updater refreshes the controller certificate when addresses change.
C5: The database accessor worker manages Dqlite cluster membership across controller nodes.
C6: Enabling high availability adds or removes controller nodes; the request goes from the client to the controller.
C7: Bootstrap provisions the controller machine from the client, installs the agent and initialises the controller records.
C8: The controller charm archive ships in the agent's data directory and is deployed at bootstrap from a local origin; if it is missing, bootstrap falls back to Charmhub.
S1: A subnet is stored as one record: its CIDR range, VLAN tag and space pointer.
S2: Zone membership records pair a zone with a subnet; the network and recovery code read them.
S3: Looking up a subnet by UUID or provider id that matches nothing fails with "subnet not found".
S4: A CIDR that is not in canonical form fails with "subnet CIDR is not valid".
S5: The provider reload discovers the cloud's spaces and subnets and adopts them into the model.
S6: The firewaller subscribes to subnet changes.
X1: A secret's metadata is one record with its owner and revisions.
X2: The permission record for a secret grant is read by cross-model relation, machine, recovery and removal code as well as the secret code.
X3: Creating a secret with a label already used within the same owner or consumer scope fails with "secret label already exists".
X4: A charm secret cannot be created with auto-prune.
X5: The rotation worker turns rotation policies into secret-rotate events for the owner.
X6: The expiry worker turns expiry times into secret-expired events.
X7: Secret backends (internal, Kubernetes, Vault) are chosen per model and used by clients and the controller.
X8: User secret commands add, update, grant, revoke and remove secrets; grants fire no hook on the observing charm.
